lines: Here's a kind of bug that never announces itself.
A recall query runs without a single complaint and hands back a tidy, confident-looking list.
Nothing about that list tells you whether it's the whole truth or just the part the query happened to be able to see.
So what's actually sitting underneath that list?
What the business asked for is one thing, and what actually happened on the floor is a separate record entirely.
And that second record never points at a recipe in the abstract. It points at one frozen version of it, because the same product made months apart can easily have been made two different ways.
Worth naming two things that sound alike but aren't.
One standard describes the equipment itself, nested several layers deep, from the whole enterprise down to a single control module.
A separate standard describes how a batch actually gets carried out, nested its own, different number of layers.
They come from related but distinct standards, and this course only claims what each one actually states on its own.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Picture rejected material getting folded back into an earlier stage of the very same production line.
Now picture a query walking lot to lot with absolutely no memory of which lots it's already passed through.
Does that query ever stop on its own?
answer: It doesn't, and the reasoning is almost mechanical once you see the loop.
Walking back into reworked material means the query can reach a lot it already counted, and with no memory of that, nothing stops it from walking the identical loop again.
Forever, not just for a while.

lines: Time to actually run it rather than just argue about it.
Take that exact unprotected version, but cap how deep it's allowed to go, just so the run itself can finish.
It doesn't taper off early. It runs straight to the cap and stops only because the cap made it stop.
That's what a query that was never going to finish on its own actually looks like from the outside.
Now the version built to actually survive that loop.
Start from one real, contaminated raw lot and trace every single thing downstream of it.
It finds everything, including the lots reachable only by passing through that rework loop once, safely, never looping a second time.
Here's where it gets uncomfortable.
Pull out exactly one real link: a single split that sent part of that contaminated lot down a second path.
Run the identical query again, and it comes back smaller.
Nothing flags it. Nothing warns anyone. Two specific, real lots simply aren't in the answer anymore.
One run always points to a frozen recipe version, never to a recipe in the abstract.
Two related standards, kept separate rather than blurred into one.
An unprotected loop that measurably never stops by itself.
And a recall that's correct with every link present, and silently short two lots the moment even one goes missing.
A recall team runs the query again after someone notices a gap and manually restores the missing link.
The second answer comes back bigger than the first.
Does that bigger second answer just mean the first one was a little short but basically fine?
answer: It doesn't, and treating it that way is the actual danger here.
Every lot the first run dropped was never recalled during the entire time the team believed that first, smaller answer was complete.
The fix was never going to be noticing a bigger number later. It's never shipping a link table with a hole in it in the first place.
